lead: Today the Church moves outward. Believers scattered by persecution reach Antioch, and some unnamed men from Cyprus and Cyrene speak of the Lord Jesus to Greeks; there the disciples are first called Christians. In the Temple at the feast of Dedication, Jesus says that no one can snatch his sheep out of his hand: “The Father and I are one.” Psalm 87 sees Zion as the mother city of all peoples, where even foreigners are counted as born.

set: Luke picks up a thread left at 8:4: the persecution after the death of Stephen scattered the believers, and they carried the word with them. Antioch on the Orontes, capital of the Roman province of Syria, was one of the largest cities of the empire, with a large Jewish community and many Gentiles drawn to the synagogue. Here, for the first time on a large scale, the Gospel is preached to Gentiles, and by ordinary believers whose names we are not told.
str: v. 19: the scattered believers speak to Jews only.
vv. 20–21: men of Cyprus and Cyrene speak to Greeks; many believe.
vv. 22–24: Jerusalem sends Barnabas; he sees grace and rejoices.
vv. 25–26: Barnabas brings Saul; a year of teaching; the name “Christians”.
kw: A real textual question. Many manuscripts read “Hellenists”, the word used in 6:1 for Greek-speaking Jews; others read “Greeks”. The contrast with v. 19 (“no one except Jews”) shows that Luke means Gentiles, and many translations, the Malayalam POC among them, say “Greeks”.

Barnabas’ name was explained as “son of encouragement” (4:36), and here he does what his name says: he “exhorted” (parekalei) them all to remain faithful. The man sent to inspect finds grace and encourages it.

A name formed like those given to the followers or household of a leader (compare “Herodians”, Mark 3:6). Many scholars think outsiders coined it. What others noticed about the disciples was that their life was about Christ.
vv: The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number became believers and turned to the Lord.
The preachers are nameless; the hand is the Lord’s. In Acts the growth of the Church is always first the Lord’s work.
When he came and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced,
A model for anyone sent to look at something new in the Church: look first for grace, and when you find it, rejoice.
it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called “Christians.”

Antioch became one of the great Churches of the ancient world. St Ignatius, its bishop early in the second century, is the first writer known to us who calls the Church “catholic” (Letter to the Smyrnaeans 8).
ch: The Church in Antioch shows what Easter does: persecution scatters, and the scattering becomes a sowing. The Church in Jerusalem does not shut down the new work; it sends a wise and generous man to strengthen it. Barnabas then goes to look for Saul, whom many still feared (9:26–27), and puts him to work. Much of the Church’s mission depends on people like Barnabas, who notice the gifts of others.

r.h: No one will snatch them out of my hand
set: The feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) recalls the cleansing and rededication of the Temple by Judas Maccabeus in 164 BC, after Antiochus IV had profaned it (1 Maccabees 4:36–59). It falls in December, so “It was winter”. Jesus walks in the portico of Solomon, the covered colonnade on the east side of the Temple court where the first believers would later gather (Acts 5:12). At the feast of the Temple’s consecration, Jesus will speak of himself as the one “whom the Father has sanctified and sent” (10:36).
str: vv. 22–24: the setting and the demand: “tell us plainly”.
vv. 25–26: works that testify, and unbelief.
vv. 27–29: the sheep hear, are known, follow, receive eternal life, and are held.
v. 30: “The Father and I are one.”
kw: The Greek name of the feast means “renewal” or “inauguration”. The Temple renewed by the Maccabees points to the new Temple, the body of Jesus (2:21).
The wolf “snatches” the sheep (10:12); no one can snatch them out of the hand of Jesus or of the Father. The believer’s security rests not on his own grip on God but on God’s grip on him.
Jesus does not say “one person” (masculine heis) but “one” in the neuter (hen): one in being and in work, while remaining Father and Son.
vv: How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Messiah, tell us plainly.
“The Jews” here are the Temple authorities and those who sided with them, as often in John (compare 9:22); Jesus and his disciples were Jews too. Jesus answers that his works have already spoken.
My sheep hear my voice. I know them, and they follow me.
Three short sentences make a whole spiritual life: listening, being known, following.
The Father and I are one.

St Augustine notes that “one” answers Arius, who made the Son less than the Father, and “are” answers Sabellius, who made Father and Son a single person (in substance). The Church’s faith holds both: one God, and distinct Persons (CCC 253–254).
ch: The Church reads this Gospel in the Easter season because the risen Shepherd keeps his promise: no one can snatch his own from his hand, not even death. This assurance is not presumption; it is hope resting on the faithfulness of God (CCC 1821). The verse “The Father and I are one” became a key text in the fourth-century defense of the true divinity of the Son, whom the Creed confesses as “consubstantial with the Father”.

qa: Does “No one will snatch them out of my hand” mean that a believer can never be lost?

No power outside us can snatch us from Christ. What remains is our own ability to stop listening and following. So the Church speaks of final perseverance as a grace we hope for and ask for, trusting in God’s faithfulness (CCC 2016).
study: Like Barnabas, do I look first for the grace of God in what is new and unfamiliar in the Church? Whose gifts could I encourage?
Which of the three, hearing his voice, being known, following, is weakest in me now?
